The three transformations explain what changes in the original statement. Equivalence explains agreement in every possible case; counterexamples explain how one case disproves an always-true claim.

Biconditionals are unpacked into two claims. Detachment explains how a fact activates a conditional, while syllogism explains how matching intermediate statements join two conditionals. Worked examples apply each method.
Detachment explicitly requires a true conditional and true hypothesis; knowing the conclusion alone is explicitly rejected.
Syllogism requires two true conditionals with matching intermediate statements. The text distinguishes a conditional conclusion from an actual event requiring p.

Counterexamples require a true hypothesis and false conclusion. Biconditionals require both directions true. The text warns that a converse need not follow from the original and that only-if does not assert the reverse.
